title: Light Theremin
intro: Wave your hand over a light sensor to play music, like a real theremin.

wiring_steps.title: The light sensor
wiring_steps.text: Unplug the USB cable before you change any wires. Plug it back in when you're done. Start with the power rails: a black wire from GND on your board to the blue (−) rail at the bottom of the breadboard, and a red wire from {{VCC}} to the red (+) rail. Push the light sensor's legs into C5 and C8 (either way round). Put the 10kΩ resistor from B8 to B12. Add a red wire from A5 to the red (+) rail, a black wire from A12 to the blue (−) rail, and a wire from {{pin:LDR_PIN}} to E8, where the sensor and resistor meet.

wiring_steps.title: The buzzer
wiring_steps.text: The buzzer sits beside the breadboard. Connect its + leg (the red wire, or the leg marked +) to {{pin:BUZZER_PIN}}, and its − leg (the black wire) to the blue (−) rail.

steps.title: Read the light
steps.text:
A light sensor (LDR) changes how easily electricity flows when light shines on it. `analogRead(LDR_PIN)` turns that into a number: bigger means brighter.

**Your task:** Run the code and open the **Serial Monitor**. Cover the sensor with your hand and watch the number drop. (In the simulator, drag the light slider.)
hints: The Serial Monitor is under your code.
In the simulator, the slider next to the light sensor changes the light.
Try the Serial Plotter tab to see it as a graph!

checks.label: Bright light gives a big number
The number changes when I cover the sensor

steps.success: Your board can see light! Analog inputs give a whole range of numbers, not just on and off.

steps.title: Test the buzzer
steps.text:
One part at a time: now the buzzer on its own. `tone(BUZZER_PIN, 440);` plays a note at 440 vibrations each second (440 Hz, the note A). `noTone` stops it.

**Your task:** fill in the blank to play the note A, then Run.

checks.label: I heard a beep every second

steps.success: Beep! Higher numbers make higher notes. Try 880: it's the same note, one octave up.

steps.title: Light becomes sound
steps.text:
Now join them: more light, higher note. `map()` turns a number from one range into another. Here it turns 0 to `ANALOG_MAX` (the sensor) into 200 to 2000 (the pitch).

**Your task:** fill in the blanks so the pitch follows the light.
hints: Read the light sensor's pin, then play the pitch you worked out.
The first blank is `LDR_PIN`, the second is a variable.

checks.label: Bright light plays a high note
The note changes when I wave my hand over the sensor

steps.success: You built an instrument! The real theremin works by sensing your hand, too.

steps.title: Hush in the dark
steps.text: **Goal:** when the sensor is fully covered (very dark), the theremin goes quiet. Otherwise it plays like before.
hints: Use an `if` to check whether `light` is very small.
Very dark could be less than `ANALOG_MAX / 10`.
Inside the `if`, use `noTone(BUZZER_PIN);`. Put the old tone code in the `else`.

checks.label: It still plays in the light
It goes quiet when I cover the sensor

steps.success: Now you can play notes and rests. That's music!

outro: Your theremin turns light into sound. You read an **analog** sensor, used **map()** to change one range of numbers into another, and played notes with **tone()**.
stretch: Play only real musical notes: pick the closest note from an array of frequencies.
Add a button that switches between two instruments (a high range and a low range).
Make the sound wobble (vibrato) by changing the pitch up and down a little, very quickly.
